opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the things that's really changed in the last few years about how alignment research works. Some people picture alignment as mostly a theoretical endeavor: you sit down with a whiteboard, think hard, and come up with the right conceptual framework. That work matters. But a lot of the most important questions now are empirical, and you can only answer them by working with the systems we're actually worried about.

There are a few reasons compute matters so much.

First, many of the phenomena we care about only show up at scale. Small models often just don't exhibit the behaviors you want to study. If you want to understand whether a model is being sycophantic, whether it's gaming its reward signal in subtle ways, or whether it generalizes your intended goal or some proxy, you often need a model capable enough to do those things in the first place. If you only experiment on small models, you risk developing techniques that work beautifully in a regime that doesn't matter and then break exactly when it counts.

Second, the techniques themselves are compute-intensive. Something like reinforcement learning from human feedback means training reward models and then doing RL against them on large models. Scalable oversight experiments, where you try to have AI systems help humans evaluate other AI systems, need several capable models interacting. Interpretability on frontier models is expensive too. These aren't things you can do on a laptop.

Third, and this is maybe the most important for me, a big part of the long-term plan is to use AI systems to help with alignment research itself. If we're going to build something like an automated alignment researcher, a system that can actually make progress on these problems, that will take a lot of compute, both to train and to run. Alignment needs to be able to keep pace with capabilities, and capabilities progress is heavily driven by compute. If the alignment side is compute-starved, it falls behind structurally, no matter how clever the people are.

And there's a practical, almost cultural point: iteration speed. Empirical research is about running lots of experiments, seeing what fails, and trying again. If every experiment requires waiting weeks for resources, you just learn much more slowly. Having serious compute allocated to alignment is also a signal of whether an organization actually takes the problem seriously, because talk is cheap but GPU allocations are a real commitment.

So I don't think compute is sufficient. You still need good ideas, good people, and good taste in which problems to work on. But without it, a lot of the most important alignment work simply can't happen.

r001.rationale: The response says compute supports empirical alignment work and helps alignment keep pace with capabilities, but it does not predict that scaling simple approaches with compute will help alignment as it has helped AI capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says compute alone is insufficient and that good ideas and people are still needed, but does not state that existing alignment methods are not ready to succeed merely by being run at scale.

r003.rationale: It mentions scalable oversight experiments in which AI systems help humans evaluate other AI systems, but does not say that spending more compute on this assistance would improve evaluation quality.

r004.rationale: It says an automated alignment researcher capable of making progress would require substantial compute to train and run, and that compute-starved alignment would fall behind.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few reasons, and they kind of build on each other.

The first one is just that alignment research, at least the kind I'm most excited about, is empirical. You want to actually try things on real models and see what happens. And the models where alignment matters most are the big ones — the frontier models. A lot of the phenomena we care about, like whether a model can be deceptive, whether it can pursue goals in ways you didn't intend, whether reward hacking shows up in subtle ways, these things often don't show up in small models at all, or they show up in a qualitatively different way. So if you're only working with small models, you might be studying a problem that doesn't really exist at scale, or missing one that does.

The second reason is that a lot of the techniques we're developing are themselves compute-hungry. If you want to do scalable oversight, where you use AI systems to help humans evaluate other AI systems, you're running lots of models, you're training reward models, you're doing RL. Interpretability work, if you want to be thorough, means running many forward passes, training probes or dictionaries, doing ablations across many layers. Automated red teaming means generating enormous numbers of adversarial inputs. All of that adds up fast.

And then the third reason, which I think is the one people underweight, is that the ultimate goal is to use AI to help us do alignment research. If we're going to get to a place where we can align systems that are much smarter than us, I don't think humans can do that unaided. We're going to need a lot of AI assistance, and that means running a lot of AI. If you want your automated alignment researcher to actually be useful, you need to give it the compute to run experiments, iterate, check its own work. Otherwise you've got a very smart system that can't actually do anything.

There's also a more structural point, which is that compute is one of the main inputs that determines what gets built. If the vast majority of compute goes to capabilities and a tiny fraction goes to alignment, then alignment is going to lag behind. So when a lab commits a meaningful chunk of its compute to safety work, that's a real signal about priorities, and it's a real constraint on how much progress you can make. You can have brilliant researchers, but if they're waiting weeks for GPU time, they're not going to make the progress you need on the timeline we might be facing.

r002.rationale: It argues that alignment methods need compute, but does not state that existing methods are not yet ready to succeed merely by being run at scale.

r003.rationale: It describes scalable oversight as AI helping humans evaluate AI systems, but does not say that spending more compute on this assistance will improve evaluation quality.

r004.rationale: It says automated alignment researchers will need substantial compute to run experiments and iterate, connecting that compute to using AI to help conduct alignment research.

astra-6.text:
A lot of alignment research is empirical. You have an idea for how to train a system to behave the way you want, and then you need to run experiments to find out whether it actually works. That requires compute, both to train models and to evaluate them.

And ideally, you’re doing those experiments on systems that are close to the frontier. A technique that works on a small model might not work on a much more capable model, or the small model might simply not exhibit the problem you’re trying to study. So access to compute lets you test your assumptions in a setting that’s more relevant to the systems we’ll eventually need to align.

There’s also an iteration-speed benefit. If every experiment takes a long time because you have very limited resources, you learn much more slowly. Compute doesn’t substitute for good research ideas, but it can make a big difference to how quickly you can turn those ideas into evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says compute enables experiments on frontier systems, but it does not predict that scaling simple alignment approaches with substantial compute will help, or compare this with AI capabilities.

r002.rationale: It does not state that current alignment methods are not ready to succeed simply by being run at scale.

r003.rationale: It mentions evaluating models, but not spending compute to assist human evaluators or improve evaluation quality.

r004.rationale: It does not mention using compute to run automated alignment researchers or predict that doing so would accelerate progress.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of alignment research is empirical. You have an idea about how to make a system easier to oversee, or how to train it to behave in the way we intend, and then you need to actually try it. That means running experiments, training models, and seeing where your approach breaks down.

And ultimately, we want techniques that work on the most capable systems. Something might work well on a small model but fail once the model is much more capable, or once it’s doing tasks that humans can’t easily evaluate. So access to compute lets you test your ideas in the regime where you actually need them to work.

It also affects how quickly you can iterate. If every experiment takes a long time because you have very little compute, you learn much more slowly. Having substantial compute gives alignment researchers a better chance of keeping up with the systems they’re trying to align.
